description_block:
BRIDGET RILEY (B. 1931)
Ka 4 
signed, titled and dated 'KA IV 1980 Riley' (on the reverse); further signed, titled and dated 'KA IV 1980 Riley' (on the stretcher bar)
oil on linen
76.2 x 67.3 cm (30 x 26 1/2in).
Painted in 1980

Provenance
Juda Rowan Gallery, London
Galerie Konstruktiv Tendens, Stockholm
Piano Nobile, London
Private Collection (acquired from the above in 2016)
Sotheby's, Hong Kong, Private Sales, 25 November 2022
Private Collection, London 

Literature
R. Kudielka, A. Tommasini & N. Naish (eds.), Bridget Riley, The Complete Paintings, Vol. II, 1974-1997, London, 2018, no.BR207 (illustrated)

The present work is the fourth in a series of eight oil paintings, plus one acrylic, titled Ka. Riley's Ka series, and her concurrent Ra works, represent the earliest paintings within the artists highly celebrated 'Egyptian palette' cycle of 1980-85. This body of work is unanimously accepted to be one of the key pivotal developments within Riley's boundary pushing contribution to 20th Century art.

As the 1970s drew to a close – Riley embarked on an extended period of travel which included a three week stay in Egypt. Her fateful visit began in Cairo, where she encountered ancient artefacts in the city's museum. She travelled through the lush farmlands of the Nile Valley, whose landscape had remained unchanged for millennia: Riley noted the distinctive strips of cultivated land, which reminded her of the horizontal planes into which the ancient Egyptians divided their paintings. Upon arriving in Luxor she observed the decorated tombs of the West Bank, and here Riley began to piece together a profound realisation. In all that she had observed, charting more than 3000 years of history, just five colours rose to prominence time and again; ochre, brick red, blue, turquoise and green – paired with white and black.

On return to her London studio, from memory Riley set about recreating the Egyptian palette with an exacting specificity. Across the 1970s Riley had favoured acrylic paint, but in order to achieve the depth of tone experienced in Egypt she returned to oil pigments for the first time in a decade. She also refined the structure of her compositions – the strength and brilliance of this new palette was not suited to the thin, delicate curves of the 1970s. Rather, stripes made a striking return, their wide, totemic forms creating a powerful sense of spatial rhythm. Each painting in the series is the result of several months' work, typically involving multiple gouache studies, collage, and the production of a full-size cartoon, before the final version was executed.

Ka 4, as is typical for the series, sees three white and three black stripes which anchor the optical timbre of the composition. Prominence is given to the tones of blue and turquoise, that shimmer as the eye skims from one to another. Six stripes of ochre and seven of brick red hover and recede. As the work oscillates between chromatic extremes, it seems to transcend its physical form, leaving behind a glowing residue of light.

While Riley never intended her titles to be descriptive, her reference to ka is nonetheless particularly evocative. The term refers to the part of the soul that—in ancient Egyptian religion—is said to survive the body after death.

BARRY FLANAGAN (1941-2009)
Cricketer 
signed with monogram and dated 'f Dec 81' (on the hare's hind quarters); further signed with monogram and numbered 'f/ 1/7' (on top of the base)
bronze with a brown patina on an integral bronze base
Height: 158.8 cm. (62 1/2 in.) (including the base)
Conceived and cast in December 1981 in an edition of 7 plus 3 artist's casts

Provenance

Exhibited

I find that the hare is a rich and expressive form that can carry the conventions of the cartoon and the attributes of the human into the animal world. So I use the hare as a vehicle to entertain. I abstract from the human figure, choosing the hare to behave as a human occasionally

(Barry Flanagan, quoted in Enrique Juncosa, Barry Flanagan Sculpture 1965-2005, exh.cat., Irish Museum of Modern Art, Dublin, 2006, p.65).

Cricketer is an iconic and early example of the most familiar vein of Flanagan's work and is accompanied by a distinguished exhibition history - with this particular cast being displayed at the British Pavilion of the 1982 Venice Biennale, as well as several further key Flanagan exhibitions.

Flanagan's bronze hares, first introduced in 1979, have become his most celebrated and sought after sculptures. They are loved by many for the expressive playfulness through which their anthropomorphic nature mirrors the viewer's own joie de vivre. At the same time, they draw on a rich tapestry of art historical notes, mythology, folklore, and autobiographical references. Flanagan recalled that his fascination with the hare began when he saw a fine specimen bounding across the Sussex Downs – an interest that was enriched by his admiration for The Leaping Hare (1972) by George Ewart Evans and David Thomson, a study of the species that weaves together legends and superstitions from around the globe together with enchanting observations from gamekeepers and poachers.

A keen sportsman and avid cricket fan, Flanagan created Cricketer in 1981, the same year England retained the Ashes after Ian Botham's remarkable match turning performance in the third Test at Headingley. The sculpture was made for Flanagan's December exhibition that winter at the Waddington Galleries—which was to be his first show composed solely of bronzes. This moment marked a seismic shift in his practice, as bronze casting soon became his preferred sculptural medium. A move which saw him rapidly receive international acclaim following the exhibition of his new bronze works at Documenta 7 in Kassel and the 1982 Venice Biennale.

Flanagan habitually returned to his works, riffing with their scale and juxtaposition to find new meaning in the familiar. This is the case with Cricketer which precipitated three further variations; The Cricketer of 1989, an almost 5 meter variation (a cast of which is in the collection of Jesus College Cambridge), The Bowler of 1990, a 3 meter cast of the hare alone, and Empire State with Bowler, Mirrored of 1997 which sees the stumps replaced by a representation of the famous building. The lithe, light-footed exuberance of the hare in Cricketer also acts as a forbearer for his Nijinsky series in which the protagonist is poised with similar athleticism.

Other casts from this edition are in the collections of the Leeds City Art Gallery and the British Council.

We are grateful to the Barry Flanagan Estate for their assistance in cataloguing this work.
